lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: know that ideas about electronic structure developed from: i an understanding that successive ionisation energies provide evidence for the existence of quantum shells and the group to which the element belongs ii an understanding that the first ionisation energy of successive elements provides evidence for electron sub-shells

primer.text: Successive ionisation energies interrogate the atom, and the atom answers in jumps. This note reads calcium's ladder as evidence for quantum shells, then applies the jump calendar to sodium, magnesium and aluminium - the position of each giant leap exposing the outer-shell count and so the group.

modules.title: Calcium's ladder of evidence
modules.opening: Successive ionisation energies are the atom's confession: where the big jumps fall, shells are exposed. This lesson reads calcium's first four ionisation energies as evidence for quantum shells and outer-shell electron counts.
keyPoints: Successive ionisation data predicts electronic configuration, outer-shell count and the group an element belongs to.
Calcium's first electron leaves easily from the 4s pair, helped by spin-pair repulsion.
The third electron comes from the 3p shell nearer the nucleus - a much bigger bill.
Large jumps between successive IEs mark shell changes; small jumps mark sub-shell changes.

low.restatement: Look for the giant leap in the IE sequence - it marks the boundary between one shell and the next.
low.analogy: It is like climbing stairs with a few cliffs: small rises are ordinary steps, cliffs are floors.
low.examPointer: The jump position gives the outer-electron count, and that count gives the group.

medium.restatement: Each successive ionisation removes an electron from an increasingly positive ion, so a smooth rise is expected; the signature is the discontinuity, whose position reveals how many electrons occupied the outer shell before the plunge inward.
medium.analogy: Peeling layers off a golf ball: the rubber layers come off with moderate effort, then the hard core stops the knife - the effort spike localises the core.
medium.examPointer: For calcium: IE1 low (4s pair repulsion), IE2 higher (no pair), IE3 a leap (3p is deeper) - the pattern reads 4s2 outer shell, group 2.

modules.title: Na, Mg, Al: the jump calendar
modules.opening: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium make the jump-calendar method routine: one jump means group 1, two mean group 2, three mean group 3. This lesson walks each element's jump position to its configuration.
keyPoints: Sodium's huge IE1-to-IE2 jump exposes one outer electron: group 1, ending in 3s1.
Magnesium's jump between IE2 and IE3 exposes two outer electrons: group 2, ending in 3s2.
Aluminium's jump between IE3 and IE4 exposes three: group 3, ending in 3s2 3p1.
The jump marks the fall from the third shell into the full, tightly-held second shell.

low.restatement: Count how many easy removals happen before the giant leap - that count is the group number.
low.analogy: It is a bus ride: flat fares for the outer seats, then a steep surcharge the moment you enter the reserved carriage.
low.examPointer: Name WHERE the jump falls (after which IE) - that is the deduction examiners mark.

medium.restatement: The jump calendar works because the first shell-change lands exactly after the outer sub-shell empties; the post-jump electrons come from the full 2p level whose shorter radius and higher effective charge raise the bill sharply.
medium.analogy: Emptying a house: rooms on the ground floor empty cheaply; the attic and the safe downstairs are a different ordeal.
medium.examPointer: For the unknown element with 899, 1757, 14850, 21005: the cliff sits between IE2 and IE3, so two outer electrons - group 2.

glossary.definition: The ordered sequence IE1, IE2, IE3... of energies for removing each next electron from an atom.
A principal energy level (n) whose boundary is exposed by the big jumps in successive ionisation data.
The highest-energy occupied quantum shell, whose electron count the position of the big jump exposes.
